title: MMLU: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
hook: Want one number for how broadly an LLM 'knows stuff'? MMLU is a 57-subject exam spanning history, law, medicine, and math — and it became a default yardstick.
key_points: A multiple-choice benchmark covering 57 subjects, from humanities to STEM to professional fields.
Tests broad knowledge and reasoning in zero- or few-shot settings, with no task-specific training.
Questions range from high-school to expert difficulty, so strong scores require real breadth.
Became one of the most-cited yardsticks for comparing large language models.
content_html: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, and colleagues built MMLU as a broad test of what a language model actually knows. It's a multiple-choice exam spanning 57 subjects — elementary math, US history, law, medicine, and many more — drawn at difficulties from high school up to expert level. Because models answer with little or no task-specific training, a high score signals genuine breadth of knowledge and reasoning, which is why MMLU became a go-to benchmark for comparing LLMs.
extra_html:
How it works

Each question is multiple choice with four options, and the model picks an answer, typically given just a few examples (few-shot) or none at all (zero-shot). Spanning 57 distinct subjects, the benchmark rewards general capability rather than a narrow skill, since you can't do well by mastering one area. Scores are reported as accuracy, and the spread across subjects also shows where a model is strong or weak. Random guessing would score around 25 percent, setting a clear floor.

Why it matters

Before benchmarks like this, comparing models often meant juggling many narrow datasets. MMLU offered a single, broad scoreboard that tracks general knowledge well, which made it a fixture in nearly every major LLM release. That popularity is double-edged: it pushed progress and gave a common language for comparison, but it also invited overfitting and contamination concerns as the same questions circulated widely. Even so, it remains a standard reference point for model capability.
